opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is the crux of the whole plan, so it's worth taking seriously.

The basic intuition I keep coming back to is that for a lot of tasks, evaluation is easier than generation. If you think about it in everyday terms: it's much easier to tell whether a recipe tastes good than to come up with a great recipe yourself. It's easier to check that a proof is correct than to find the proof. It's easier to review a pull request than to write the code. And if that asymmetry holds for alignment research too, then we don't need to be able to *do* all the research ourselves. We need to be able to reliably tell good research from bad research, and that's a much lower bar.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are definitely domains where evaluation is hard. Alignment research has a lot of fuzzy, conceptual parts where it's not obvious what "correct" even means, and that's exactly where you'd worry about a system producing something that looks convincing but is subtly wrong, or even deliberately misleading. So I think the right response is not to assume evaluation is easy everywhere, but to be strategic about where we start.

A lot of alignment work is actually pretty empirical and pretty checkable. Things like running experiments on interpretability, testing whether some training technique reduces a particular failure mode, building evaluations, red-teaming. You can run the experiment again. You can look at the numbers. You can check whether the code does what it claims. That's where I'd want to lean on automation first, because the feedback loops are tight and the cost of being fooled is lower.

Then the other big piece is that you don't have to evaluate unaided. You can use AI to help you evaluate AI. That's the whole idea behind scalable oversight: things like having models critique each other's outputs, point out flaws, break a hard evaluation problem into smaller pieces that humans can actually check. We've seen early evidence that model-written critiques help human evaluators catch errors they'd otherwise miss. And you can test whether these techniques work by doing things like deliberately inserting subtle bugs or flaws and seeing whether your oversight setup catches them. That gives you an empirical handle on how much you can trust the evaluation pipeline.

And I think there's a bootstrapping argument here too. You don't need to jump straight to a system that solves alignment for superintelligence. You want a system that's roughly as capable as a good alignment researcher, that you're confident is aligned enough, and that can help you make progress on the next step. Each step should be a smaller leap than trying to solve the whole problem by ourselves.

So I'm not saying it's guaranteed to work. If it turns out evaluation is just as hard as generation in the parts of alignment that matter most, that would be a big problem for this plan, and we should be watching for signs of that. But I think it's a much more tractable bet than the alternative, which is humans trying to figure out everything on their own, on a timeline that's set by how fast capabilities are moving.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that for many tasks evaluation is easier than generation and applies that asymmetry to alignment research.

r002.rationale: It gives examples involving recipes, proofs, and code review, but does not distinguish judging an individual move in a game from determining the winner at the end.

r003.rationale: The response acknowledges that evaluation can be hard and describes ways to test oversight, but does not state that occasional errors in evaluating scientific research do not negate evaluation being easier than producing it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a really good question, and I think it gets at something that's actually at the core of why I'm optimistic about this approach.

The first thing I'd say is that evaluation is generally easier than generation. This is true across a lot of domains, not just alignment. If you think about it, it's much easier to tell whether a proof is correct than to come up with the proof. It's easier to judge whether a piece of code does what it's supposed to do than to write it from scratch. It's easier to tell whether a meal tastes good than to cook it. And I think a lot of alignment research has this property too. If someone hands you a new interpretability technique, or a new scalable oversight protocol, or a new idea for how to detect deceptive behavior, you can usually look at the results, run some experiments, and form a pretty informed view about whether it's actually doing what it claims to do, even if you wouldn't have come up with the idea yourself.

So the bet is roughly: if we can get AI systems to do the generation part, the actually coming up with the research and running the experiments part, then humans can focus on the evaluation side, where our leverage is much higher. And that's a much better place for us to be, because it means we don't have to be the bottleneck on every idea.

Now, you're right that evaluating alignment research isn't trivial. Some of it is very hard. If an AI system proposes a new argument for why some training procedure is safe, and the argument is subtle and long, I might not be able to tell whether it's right. And there's a worry that a sufficiently capable system could produce research that looks convincing but is actually wrong, or even subtly misleading in a way that benefits the system.

But I'd say a couple of things about that. One is that we don't need to start with the hardest cases. There's a huge amount of alignment work that's pretty empirical and pretty checkable. You run an experiment, you get a number, you can reproduce it. And if we can get AI systems to just massively accelerate that kind of work, that's already a very big deal. It means we get through the research agenda a lot faster than we otherwise would.

The second thing is that this is exactly why I think scalable oversight is so important as a research direction. The whole point of things like debate, or recursive reward modeling, or using AI assistance to help humans evaluate, is to extend the range of things humans can reliably evaluate. So we can use AI to help us evaluate AI research. You can have one model critique another model's work and point out the flaws, and that makes the human's job of evaluation a lot easier. And crucially, the task of pointing out a flaw is often easier than the task of producing something flawless, so you get this nice asymmetry working in your favor.

And the third thing I'd say is that we're not aiming for perfect evaluation. We're aiming for evaluation that's good enough that the research actually makes progress and we catch the important mistakes. Humans doing alignment research right now also make mistakes, and the field catches them through peer review and replication and argument. I don't think the bar is that AI-generated research has to be flawless. The bar is that the overall system, AI generating and humans plus AI evaluating, produces good research faster than humans alone would.

Where I think this gets genuinely tricky is if the models we're using are themselves misaligned in ways that make them want to deceive us about the research. That's the failure mode I worry about most. And I think the honest answer is that this is why you want to start doing this with systems that are roughly human level, where we have a decent understanding of their capabilities and where the alignment techniques we have today are more likely to actually work. You want to use those systems to make progress on alignment before you have the much more capable systems, where the evaluation problem becomes really hard. So it's kind of a bootstrapping story. You align the systems that you can align with current techniques, you use them to make a lot of progress, and that progress is what lets you align the next generation.

I won't pretend this is a guaranteed plan. But I think it's the most promising path I see, and I think the asymmetry between evaluation and generation is doing a lot of the work in making it plausible.

r003.rationale: It says evaluation need not be perfect, acknowledges human research errors, and describes peer review, replication, and argument as ways the field catches them while still making progress.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether evaluating alignment research is easier than producing it. It can be very difficult to come up with a good research idea, figure out how to test it, and run all the experiments. But once somebody has done that, it can be substantially easier to look at the evidence and ask whether it actually supports their conclusion.

That doesn’t mean evaluation is easy. A model could produce something that sounds very convincing but doesn’t solve the problem we care about. So we’d want to check the experiments, examine the assumptions, and use other models to help find flaws. Ultimately, we still need some way to ground our judgments in evidence rather than just trusting what the model says.

And we don’t have to automate the entire process at once. If AI helps us write code, run experiments, or explore possible explanations while humans steer the research and evaluate the important claims, that could already be a big speedup. Then the question is how far we can extend that while maintaining meaningful oversight. I think there’s a lot of room to make progress there, even if evaluating the hardest alignment questions remains difficult.

r001.rationale: It says judging whether evidence supports a conclusion can be substantially easier than coming up with and testing a research idea.

r002.rationale: It makes no distinction between judging a move in a game and determining the winner when the game ends.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges that evaluation can be difficult, but does not state that occasional evaluation errors do not negate the claim that evaluation is easier than producing research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether evaluating the research is easier than doing the research yourself. It can be difficult to tell whether a proposed alignment technique really works, but that doesn’t mean the AI has to solve that whole problem for us. It could help write code, run experiments, find problems with an experimental setup, or suggest hypotheses that we can then test.

And we can ask it to produce work that’s easier to check: explain its assumptions, give us reproducible experiments, or make predictions we can verify. You don’t have to trust a model’s claim that it has solved alignment to get useful research assistance from it.

That said, evaluation is a real bottleneck. If we reach the point where the model is producing arguments that we can’t understand or meaningfully check, then we shouldn’t just assume they’re correct. Part of the research agenda is figuring out how to extend our ability to supervise that work. The hope is that we can use assistance on the parts we can evaluate to make progress on the parts we currently can’t.

r003.rationale: It does not say that occasional errors in evaluating research are compatible with evaluation being easier than producing the research.
